summary: The spongy moth is a non-native moth whose caterpillars eat the leaves of many New York trees, especially oaks. Its populations rise and fall in cycles of roughly 10 to 15 years, and outbreaks usually end on their own through disease and predators. Most trees can survive two or three years in a row of losing their leaves; trees die mainly when other stresses, like disease or other insects, hit them in the same years. DEC says spongy moths do not pose a major threat to New York's forests overall.
history: The spongy moth comes from France. It was accidentally brought to the United States in 1869, and some escaped and started the first U.S. population in Medford, Massachusetts.
seasons: Egg masses look like light-brown, fuzzy or spongy patches on tree trunks and other surfaces, each holding 600 to 700 eggs; they can be found from about August through April. In spring, tiny black caterpillars hatch and eat tender new leaves, growing to about 2.5 inches. They turn into moths in late June and early July: the females cannot fly, while males are often seen flying in summer and fall.

handling.text: Do not touch the caterpillars without protection: their hairs can cause mild to moderate skin irritation in some people, especially in late spring and early summer when caterpillars are hatching and growing. On your own property, DEC says egg masses can be destroyed by scraping them off into a container of detergent. In New York City parks like Kissena, park rules forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest or eggs.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks like Kissena Park, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
